Social Security budget: deputies and senators fail to agree, Lecornu can now govern by ordinance

On Thursday, November 26, seven deputies and seven senators meeting in a joint committee failed to reach a compromise on the 2027 Social Security budget [1]. The bill returns to the National Assembly on December 7 [2][3], and the government now has the right to enact it by ordinance [3].
The joint committee (CMP) brings together seven deputies and seven senators to write a common version when the two chambers disagree [1]. It broke up on Thursday without an agreement [1][3].

The general rapporteur from Les Républicains, Thibault Bazin, sees common ground on about a hundred articles, but around ten remain in dispute [2][3]. He asked the government to open “real” negotiations [3].

The government wants to cut the Social Security deficit from €21.8 billion in 2026 to €12.7 billion in 2027; the version passed by the Senate puts it at €14 billion [4][5]. Senators had adopted the bill on November 18 by 201 votes to 124 [6].

The 50-day deadline set by the Constitution expired this Thursday: past that point, the executive can implement its budget by ordinance, meaning it can apply its original bill without a final vote [3].

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu reacted on X: the points of agreement “must serve as the basis for building a compromise” [7]. At the Mayors' Congress, he said: “If no one takes responsibility, will I take mine?”, before answering yes [7].

According to AFP, he seems to prefer Article 49.3, which passes a bill without a vote unless a no-confidence motion brings down the government, over ordinances, which he describes as “an emergency reserve parachute, a tool for extreme urgency” [8][7].
The Socialists, who let the Social Security budget through last year, seem less willing to do so this time; LFI deputy Anaïs Belouassa-Cherifi says her group will vote against it [3].
Key takeaway: without a majority in the Assembly, the government has only two tools left to give Social Security a budget, Article 49.3 or ordinances, and both are politically risky [3][8].

The difference matters. According to L'Express, Article 49.3 allows amendments voted by deputies to be kept, a gesture toward the opposition, but it exposes the government to a no-confidence vote; with ordinances, a no-confidence motion does not bring down the budget [9]. For the state budget, this route only opens 70 days after the bill is tabled, around December 17 [9].
The state budget is following a parallel path: the Senate is debating it in plenary session and is due to vote on the whole bill on December 9 [10].

The Social Security budget decides what you pay in contributions, how much of your healthcare is reimbursed and how retirement pensions change. Until it is passed, these rules for 2027 remain uncertain, and the government may end up imposing them without a vote by deputies.

Ukraine: Zelensky warns of a new major Russian attack on electricity, Trump's envoy praises Putin's “restraint”

On Thursday, November 26, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia is preparing a new massive attack on Ukraine's energy, logistics and vital services [1]. The same day, US envoy Jared Kushner said Vladimir Putin had “shown restraint” and wanted peace [1][2].

According to AP, Zelensky warned on Thursday that Moscow is preparing a new large-scale strike targeting the country's energy infrastructure, logistics and essential services, as winter sets in [1][2].

Jared Kushner, who leads the US mediation with Steve Witkoff, said Putin had shown “restraint” by agreeing not to use nuclear weapons, and that he believes the Russian president wants peace [1]. He says he is preparing the next round of three-way talks between Americans, Russians and Ukrainians [1].

Donald Trump wrote on social media on Thursday that he wants Putin to “withdraw all military aggression against territories across Europe”, in the hope that a deal between Russia and Ukraine is reached “quickly” [1].

Russia's top diplomat, Sergei Lavrov, said on Thursday that Washington is approaching the negotiations with an understanding of the need to eliminate the “root causes” of the conflict, Moscow's phrase for its demands on Ukraine and NATO [1].

On November 19 in Shenzhen, China, after the APEC summit and his meetings with Trump and Xi Jinping, Putin had refused to negotiate a limited ceasefire, following Ukrainian strikes on the Crimean Bridge [3]. He had promised a response “far more painful” than the damage suffered by the bridge [3][4].
According to the Russian agency TASS, Putin had nevertheless asked his Security Council to study partial truces, including a halt to strikes on energy and a ceasefire at sea [4].
Key takeaway: while Trump's envoys talk about peace, the war is intensifying on the ground, and winter makes Ukraine's power grid a priority target [1][3].

The Crimean Bridge, which links the annexed peninsula to Russia, is a symbol: part of its roadway collapsed after a Ukrainian Flamingo missile strike, and the parallel railway was hit by Neptune missiles, which stopped the trains [4]. Moscow says it is purely civilian; Kyiv shows images of Russian tanks using it [4].

The war is already spilling over into neighboring countries: Poland has asked NATO to be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles over Ukraine [5]. On the money side, Europeans have pushed back to December their decision on a €45 billion loan to Kyiv [6].

Massive strikes on Ukraine's electricity force the country to seek power and gas from its European neighbors, which can weigh on the energy prices you pay. And Europe, France included, finances a large part of Ukraine's resistance.

Yemen: after the deadly strike on the Jazan refinery, the Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed 50 Houthi targets, the rebels count 19 civilians killed in two days

On Thursday, November 26, the Saudi-led coalition announced it had destroyed 50 military targets of the Houthi rebels in three Yemeni provinces, including that of the capital Sanaa. It is retaliating for a series of Houthi attacks on ports, refineries and the Saudi capital [1][2][3].
The coalition's spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, speaks of 50 “legitimate military targets” in the provinces of Sanaa, Hodeidah (west) and Saada (northwest), without specifying what they were [1].

The coalition also says it destroyed a ballistic missile launcher in Hodeidah that was allegedly used to strike the Aramco refinery in Jazan [3]. That strike killed a Nepali worker on Thursday, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry [6].
Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes near Sanaa airport, where an AFP journalist saw smoke [1].
The Houthi-run Health Ministry says at least 19 civilians were killed and 25 injured in 48 hours. Their army counts 109 Saudi strikes in 24 hours. CNN was unable to verify these figures [2].

On Wednesday the 25th, the coalition issued an evacuation warning and then struck the port of Hodeidah, through which 80% of Yemen's humanitarian aid and 70% of its commercial imports pass [4]. The Houthis targeted the Saudi port of Jizan; the coalition says it shot down a drone over the port of Jeddah and intercepted missiles aimed at Riyadh [5].

On November 24, London froze the Houthi movement's assets and imposed travel bans on four of its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim al-Houthi, citing attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure [7].
Key takeaway: the war between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis has flared up again, and each side is now targeting the other's ports and energy [1][4][5].

The escalation follows a chain of threats. On November 20, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree had promised to strike Jeddah and the other ports on the Saudi west coast if Hodeidah was bombed, and warned that Saudi airspace was no longer safe for civilian aircraft [8]. Hodeidah was hit on the 25th, and so was Jizan [4][5].
For Yemenis, striking Hodeidah means hitting the entry point for food and medicine in a country already devastated by years of war [4].
For the rest of the world, the threat hangs over the Red Sea: the Houthis are now targeting Saudi ports on that coast, such as Jeddah and Jizan, in addition to refineries [5][8].

Part of the goods arriving in Europe from Asia pass through the Red Sea. If the fighting spreads to ports and ships, shipping companies may once again sail around Africa, which lengthens journeys and can make what you buy more expensive.

news.2026-11-27-japon-inflation-tokyo-ba: Japan: Tokyo inflation at a 16-month high, the Bank of Japan moves closer to a rate hike on December 18

Consumer prices excluding fresh food rose 2.9% year on year in November in Tokyo, their biggest increase since July 2025, Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs announced on Friday, November 27. The figure strengthens the case for a Bank of Japan rate hike as early as December [1][2].

The Tokyo index, released three weeks before the national figure, serves as a barometer for the whole country [1]. Excluding fresh food, it reached 2.9%, slightly below the expected 3.0%; headline inflation is 2.8% [2].
The Bank of Japan's (BoJ) policy rate, the rate at which it lends to banks, is 1.25% [4]. According to a Reuters poll, 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17-18 meeting [4].
Governor Kazuo Ueda repeated on November 18 and 19 that the bank would keep raising rates if conditions warrant, and warned that underlying inflation could exceed the 2% target [3].

But households are struggling: on November 24, the government downgraded its assessment of consumption for the first time since February 2024, because of rising prices [5]. It did, however, upgrade its view of exports, for the first time since June, thanks to sales to the United States and the EU [5].

On Thursday, November 26, Tokyo protested against the US plan to impose a 15% tariff on its products over “overcapacity”: government spokesman Minoru Kihara said Japan has no such practices, even though the rate matches the deal already concluded [6].
Key takeaway: Japan keeps raising rates to curb inflation, and December could mark a new step [3][4].

In December 2025, the BoJ had already raised its rate to the highest level since 1995 [7]. Yet the yen fell right after that hike, because markets found the bank's message too vague about what would come next [8].

The same risk exists this time: the US Federal Reserve is also raising rates, so the yield gap in favor of the dollar remains large. Analysts expect the dollar to stay close to 160 yen as long as the BoJ does not speed up or the Fed does not pause [4][8].
The BoJ therefore has to choose between two risks: letting inflation run, or slowing already fragile consumption [3][5].

When Japanese rates rise, investing money in Japan becomes more profitable, and some of the Japanese capital invested abroad may return home, which can shake global markets, and therefore your savings invested in the stock market. And as long as the yen stays weak, a trip to Japan costs you less in euros.

Banks: final green light for UniCredit, the Italian lender takes control of Commerzbank and wants to install its CEO Andrea Orcel as board chairman

On Thursday, November 26, Italian bank UniCredit announced that all conditions of its offer for Germany's Commerzbank have been met, after the final green light from the Polish regulator. It immediately called for an extraordinary general meeting to replace nine of the ten board members and install its CEO Andrea Orcel as chairman of the supervisory board [1][2][3].

The last approval came from the KNF, Poland's financial watchdog: it concerns the indirect change of control of Commerzbank's operations in Poland, including mBank, 69.1% owned by the German group [1][2].

UniCredit said it had not waived any condition of its offer [2]. The new UniCredit shares, given in exchange for the Commerzbank shares tendered, are due to reach shareholders' accounts by December 7, 2026 at the latest [1][4].

The exchange offer, which closed in July, had collected 17.6% of Commerzbank's capital; with its direct stake of 26.77% and 3.22% in derivatives, UniCredit reached 47.59% of the capital and 49.65% of the voting rights [4].

The Italian bank is proposing ten candidates for the supervisory board, with Andrea Orcel then due to become its chairman, subject to the regulators' fit-and-proper assessment [5]. Commerzbank replied that it will review the request and convene the meeting if the legal conditions are met [2].
The meeting could be held in early January according to dpa-AFX, or in the first quarter of 2027 according to other sources; no date has been set [5][6].
On the stock market, Commerzbank shares were down 3.39% on Thursday morning, at €33.34 [5].
The German state remains: it still holds about 13.3% of Commerzbank, and the question of that stake remains open, according to Euronews [1].

Key takeaway: this ends a saga lasting more than two years and is one of the largest cross-border banking combinations in Europe. An Italian bank is taking control of Germany's second-largest private bank, despite opposition from its management, which recommended rejecting the offer until the very end [7].

It all began in September 2024: Berlin was selling part of its Commerzbank shares, inherited from the 2008 bailout, and UniCredit snapped up 4.49% of the capital for about €702 million, at €13.20 per share, then bought as much again on the market to reach about 9% [8][9]. The German government had been caught off guard [9].

For Europe, it is a test of the “banking union”: Brussels and the ECB have argued for years for bigger banks able to compete with US giants, but governments often defend their national champions. Spain showed this in 2025 with BBVA's failed bid for Sabadell [10].

The battle is not over: UniCredit now has to take control of the supervisory board, and going above 50% of the voting rights could force it to make an offer for the rest of mBank's shares in Poland [2].

If you are a customer of Commerzbank or its online subsidiary in Germany, nothing changes for your account in the short term. If you tendered Commerzbank shares to the offer, you will receive UniCredit shares by December 7 [1]. More broadly, bigger European banks can lend more to businesses, but competition between banks decreases.

How it works: an exchange offer and taking control of a board

UniCredit did not pay for Commerzbank in euros: it made an exchange offer, meaning new UniCredit shares for each Commerzbank share tendered [4]. The buyer thus keeps its cash, but the target's shareholders become shareholders of the buyer. An offer only goes through once all its conditions, including green lights from regulators in each country concerned, are met: the last one was Polish, because of mBank [1]. In Germany, a listed company has two bodies: a management board that runs it and a supervisory board that oversees and appoints it. Whoever controls the supervisory board therefore controls the bank: that is why UniCredit is calling for an extraordinary general meeting to place its candidates there [5]. The target's share price often falls once the offer is completed, because the “speculation premium” disappears.
Precedents: major banking maneuvers in Europe
September 11, 2024
UniCredit buys 4.49% of Commerzbank from the German state for about €702 million, at €13.20 per share, above the closing price of €12.60, and rises to about 9% of the capital [8][9].
A surprise stake-building can launch a takeover bid more than two years before its outcome.
October 16-17, 2025
Spanish bank BBVA's offer for Sabadell fails: only 25.47% of the voting rights are tendered, below the 30% threshold; Sabadell shares fall 6.8% and BBVA gains about 7% in New York [10][11].
Without the support of the target's shareholders and facing a hostile government, a bank bid can fail; the market welcomed the withdrawal on the buyer's side.
July 2026
End of UniCredit's exchange offer: 17.6% of Commerzbank's capital tendered, giving control of 47.59% of the capital with the direct stake and derivatives [4].
You can take de facto control without exceeding 50% of the capital, provided you then win over the regulators and the board.

news.2026-11-27-indonesie-ocde-msci.titl: Indonesia: Prabowo hosts the OECD chief to speed up membership, while MSCI keeps up the threat to downgrade the Jakarta stock market
news.2026-11-27-indonesie-ocde-msci.summ: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto received OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann in Jakarta to review the country's bid to join this club of developed countries [1]. At the same time, stock index provider MSCI is threatening to downgrade the Indonesian stock market [3].
news.2026-11-27-indonesie-ocde-msci.poin: Jakarta wants to use membership of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to reform its education, healthcare and anti-corruption efforts [2].

On November 24, MSCI denied any softening: its plan to move Indonesia from “emerging” market status to “standalone” market status remains on the table [3]. The consultation is open until April 30, with a decision by June 30 at the latest [3].
According to Bloomberg, MSCI's CEO, Henry Fernandez, and Prabowo had nevertheless spoken for more than an hour on November 10 [4].
One broker estimates that $11 billion in foreign capital could leave the country in the event of a downgrade; the Jakarta index remains nearly 10% below its level before the warning [3].
Key takeaway: Indonesia's credibility with investors is at stake: the OECD would be a seal of good governance, an MSCI downgrade the opposite signal [1][3].
Many funds track MSCI indices: leaving the “emerging” category would push them to sell Indonesian shares [3].
news.2026-11-27-indonesie-ocde-msci.forM: If your savings include an “emerging markets” fund, it probably holds Indonesian shares: a downgrade would push them out of it.

news.2026-11-27-inde-pib-attendu-7-6.tit: India: growth expected at 7.6% this summer thanks to investment, official verdict on November 30
news.2026-11-27-inde-pib-attendu-7-6.sum: Rating agency India Ratings and Research (Ind-Ra) forecasts that the Indian economy grew 7.6% in the July-September quarter, driven mainly by investment, it said on Thursday, November 26. The official figure comes out on November 30 [2][1].
news.2026-11-27-inde-pib-attendu-7-6.poi: Other economists expect growth of between 7.4% and 7.8% for this second quarter of the 2026-2027 fiscal year [2].
According to Ind-Ra, investment, meaning spending by companies and the state to build factories and roads or buy machinery, is driving growth [2].
The Statistics Ministry (MoSPI) will publish the GDP figure, the wealth produced in the country, on November 30 [2].
According to Business Today magazine, growth should stay above 7% despite headwinds [1].
news.2026-11-27-inde-pib-attendu-7-6.why: Key takeaway: India would keep a growth pace of around 7.5%, while China, according to the firm Capital Economics, barely exceeded 2.4% in October [2][3].

This contrast fuels foreign investors' interest in India, presented as an alternative to China for producing goods and investing money. Investment-driven growth is also more solid than growth driven by consumption alone [2].
news.2026-11-27-inde-pib-attendu-7-6.for: A fast-growing India is an ever-bigger market for European companies that sell there, and therefore means jobs and orders all the way to France.
